Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost

Threat.value: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.

issues.item: Triggers: Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, the trigger set is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile: darkness and especially tactile/unexpected touch are more characteristic of direct interpersonal assault than of a loved-one trauma, and there is no accompanying memory or appraisal content that links touch or darkness to this trauma.

The lock-checking threat item and parallel checking-locks strategy suggest a home-intrusion or direct personal danger formulation. In a loved-one trauma profile, this can occur, but here it is not supported by any appraisals or memory content about preventing another loss, danger to family, or responsibility. As selected, these items pull toward a different trauma narrative than the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Tactile (Unexpected Touch): Being touched unprepared
issues.explanation: Within the allowed nodes, the strongest coherence is around hyperarousal and intrusive memory, but the specific combination of tactile triggers plus lock-checking behavior is difficult to explain as one coherent formulation for a loved-one trauma without any linked negative appraisal content. This is more than merely unusual because the selected items imply different threat contexts.

The trigger/threat pattern is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of trauma to a loved one. Tactile unexpected-touch triggers plus broad startle to nearby movement are more typical of direct assault or personal threat trauma, not bereavement-focused trauma, unless there is additional context not represented elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Tactile (Unexpected Touch): Being touched unprepared
issues.explanation: Door/lock checking and hypervigilant startle responses imply an ongoing fear of intruders or immediate physical attack, but the rest of the profile centers on intrusive memory and loss-related trigger content rather than a coherent physical-danger narrative tied to the loved-one trauma.

issues.item: Threat: Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
issues.explanation: Within the formulation, Threat is strongly linked to Triggers and Maladaptive Strategies, but the selected threat items reflect personal safety/intruder danger whereas the only clearly trauma-congruent trigger is loss-themed conversation. This creates a poor match between the active nodes: the threat content does not plausibly arise from the listed trauma-relevant triggers.

issues.item: Triggers: Tactile (Unexpected Touch): Being touched unprepared
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, tactile triggering by unexpected touch is not impossible, but paired with the rest of this profile it implies a direct personal-assault or physical-threat theme that is not supported by the memory items or the loss-focused trigger item. This makes the trigger set clinically incoherent around the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Threat: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: Repeated door/window lock checking suggests an ongoing home-intrusion or personal safety threat appraisal. In a profile centered on trauma to a loved one, with memory items focused on reliving and no appraisals linking the event to current intruder danger, this threat item does not fit the dominant loss-based formulation and appears mismatched with the other selected items.

issues.item: Checking Locks: repeatedly check locks, doors, or windows
issues.explanation: Repeatedly checking locks/doors/windows is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile and the indexed trauma type (trauma to a loved one). The other selected items center on grief/loss reminders, intrusive vivid replay, and generalized startle, but do not indicate a home-intrusion, assault, or safety-compulsion theme that would make lock-checking a coherent trauma-linked strategy. As selected, this item appears to target a threat-management pattern not otherwise represented in triggers, memory, or appraisals.

vignette: John is a 48-year-old North American man who owns a small shop in his neighborhood. He has been married for nearly two decades to Sarah, with whom he shares a life of mutual support and love. Despite their deep connection, the shadow of a traumatic event has cast an enduring pall over John’s life. The trauma began when John witnessed a car accident that took the life of his younger brother, Mark, who was driving home from work one evening. The image of Mark's car flipping and crashing into a tree remains vividly etched in John's memory. He remembers the sound of sirens growing louder as he rushed to the scene, only to see emergency services struggling to extricate Mark from the wreckage. This event has left John with persistent triggers that are intricately tied to his daily life. John finds himself unable to watch news reports or movies where characters experience loss or witness tragic events. The mere mention of a funeral can send waves of anxiety through him, and he avoids funerals altogether. Recently, his niece was involved in a minor car accident, which triggered another episode of acute distress for John. He had to leave the room during discussions about her safety, unable to bear even the indirect association with tragedy. To cope, John has developed several maladaptive strategies that have become habitual over time. He smokes heavily, often lighting up a cigarette whenever he feels overwhelmed by intrusive thoughts or memories. This behavior has led to noticeable health concerns and tensions within his marriage, as Sarah worries about his well-being but understands the depth of his distress. John also avoids thinking about the traumatic event itself by distracting himself with work. As a shopowner, he keeps busy managing inventory, interacting with customers, and handling finances. However, the constant busyness has taken a toll on his relationship with Sarah; he often comes home late or is preoccupied during family time. Sarah has expressed her concerns about feeling neglected and emotionally distant. John’s avoidance of grief reminders extends to anything that might evoke memories of Mark. He refrains from visiting cemeteries, even for important family gatherings, and avoids any discussions about his brother with friends or colleagues. This withdrawal has led to a sense of isolation, as he feels increasingly disconnected from both his community and Sarah. The trauma manifests in John’s daily life through exaggerated startle responses. Ordinary sounds like the chime of the shop door opening or a loud noise on the street can cause him to jump in alarm, his heart racing with fear. Unexpected movements, such as a sudden shadow cast by a passing vehicle or a neighbor's unexpected knock at the door, trigger intense reactions that leave John feeling jumpy and unsafe. John is plagued by strong negative emotions—fear, horror, anger, guilt, and shame—that are intertwined with his memories of Mark’s accident. He often feels like he failed to prevent the tragedy, even though there was nothing he could have done at the time. This guilt has made him hyper-vigilant about potential dangers around him, leading to a heightened sense of threat in everyday situations. The memory of the event replays vividly and constantly, as if it were happening in real-time rather than being a past occurrence. John relives the moment when he saw Mark's car crash, his brother’s face frozen in terror, and the sound of sirens growing louder. These memories feel so immediate that they disrupt his daily life, making it difficult to focus on work or engage fully with Sarah. John had come to believe that avoiding triggers and distracting himself with work were the only ways to cope, but these strategies have left him feeling increasingly isolated and overwhelmed. What frightened John most was the thought of losing control in front of customers at the shop or being unable to function at all due to his overwhelming anxiety. It was a particularly harrowing night when he found himself paralyzed by fear while locking up the shop late one evening, that finally pushed John to seek help. He realized that his avoidance and maladaptive strategies were not sustainable, and he was most hopeful for finding ways to manage his symptoms so he could reconnect with Sarah and lead a more fulfilling life. John's current state reflects the culmination of months of distress, where the trauma has seeped into every aspect of his daily existence. He is now seeking therapy to regain control over his reactions and find healthier coping mechanisms that will allow him to move forward without losing touch with those he loves most.
